claims.text: The target material is an Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a continuous dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The alloy exhibits catastrophic interfacial cracking and low room-temperature ductility because stress concentrates at phase boundaries.
Severe plastic deformation at 0.4–0.5 Tm will introduce a high dislocation density and break the continuity of the eutectic lamellae.
A subsequent anneal above 2 GPa will promote partial recrystallization and stabilize the fragmented lamellar pattern.
For this alloy, 0.4–0.5 Tm corresponds approximately to 600–800 °C.
The treatment will transform continuous lamellae into a patterned, fragmented, or equiaxed structure.
The transformed structure will have a high density of high-angle grain boundaries and a reduced interfacial aspect ratio.
High-angle grain boundaries and shortened interfaces will impede crack propagation and dissipate dislocation pile-ups.
High-pressure annealing will permit recrystallization and grain-boundary migration without allowing brittle continuous eutectic lamellae to reform.
Extreme pressure suppresses void nucleation in this alloy.
Extreme pressure stabilizes the fragmented microstructure against coarsening.
The patterned microstructure will enable strain hardening and thereby decouple the strength-ductility trade-off.
The treatment will produce more than 10% room-temperature tensile elongation and more uniform plasticity.
The treatment will reduce catastrophic interfacial cracking.
Yield strength will be maintained or slightly increased relative to the as-cast lamellar state.
Conventional HIP at 100–200 MPa typically relieves internal stresses but does not fundamentally alter the lamellar morphology or arrest interfacial cracking in this alloy.
A pressure above 2 GPa is the critical threshold for suppressing void nucleation and stabilizing the fragmented microstructure.
Below the proposed pressure threshold, the material may revert to a brittle lamellar state or undergo pressure-related phase instability.
Excessive treatment temperature or time may permit eutectic reformation, phase-fraction changes, or excessive grain growth.
